body.text: IRS Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, is the form U.S. businesses use to compute and claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 using the Regular Credit or Alternative Simplified Credit method. The revised form requires Sections E and F from 2024, while Section G component-level reporting becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025.
Executive Summary and Regulatory Evolution of Form 6765

Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 6765, officially titled Credit for Increasing Research Activities, serves as the mandatory statutory and procedural instrument through which United States taxpayers compute, substantiate, and claim the federal research and development (R&D) tax credit established under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). Historically utilized primarily as a quantitative computational schedule for aggregating research expenditures and calculating incremental credit yields, Form 6765 has undergone a comprehensive structural overhaul across the 2024, 2025, and 2026 filing cycles.

This administrative transformation shifts federal R&D tax compliance away from high-level, year-end cost-center expense aggregation toward granular, component-level technical and financial substantiation reported directly on the tax return. Driven by the phased introduction of Item A, Item B, Section E (Other Information), Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary), and Section G (Business Component Information) on the revised Form 6765, the regulatory framework requires taxpayers to establish an explicit, verifiable nexus between Qualified Research Expenditures (QREs) and discrete qualifying business components satisfying the conjunctive Four-Part Test of IRC Section 41(d) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a).
Statutory Architecture of Form 6765 and IRC Section 41
Procedural Function and Entity-Level Compliance

Form 6765 operates as the mandatory procedural bridge connecting an enterprise's technical research execution to the dollar-for-dollar federal tax liability reduction authorized under IRC Section 41 and incorporated into the General Business Credit under IRC Section 38. Unlike ordinary business expense deductions or capital amortization allowances under IRC Sections 174 or 174A—which reduce gross income to arrive at taxable income and therefore deliver a cash-tax benefit proportional to the taxpayer's marginal income tax rate—the Section 41 research credit directly offsets federal income tax liability dollar for dollar, or, for eligible early-stage enterprises electing under IRC Section 41(h), offsets federal employer payroll tax liability under IRC Section 3111(f).

Beyond arithmetic computation, Form 6765 serves as the legally binding evidentiary record for three foundational tax elections that govern credit monetization, controlled group allocation, and expenditure recovery. First, regarding calculation methodology selection, taxpayers must compute their credit entitlement under either the Regular Credit Method in Section A (Lines 1–13, codified under IRC Section 41(a)(1) and Section 41(c)(1)–(3)) or the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Method in Section B (Lines 14–26, codified under IRC Section 41(c)(4) and regulated under 26 CFR § 1.41-9). Second, regarding the reduced credit election under IRC Section 280C(c)(2), taxpayers must check "Yes" or "No" in Item A at the top of page 1 of the revised Form 6765 to document whether they irrevocably elect the reduced research credit on their original, timely filed tax return (including extensions). This election directly governs whether the taxpayer preserves its full domestic research deduction or capital account balance under IRC Section 174A (and prior IRC Section 174) or must reduce its deductible or capitalized domestic research expenditures by the full amount of the gross credit claimed. Third, regarding the Qualified Small Business (QSB) payroll tax offset, eligible startup entities meeting the gross receipts and age criteria of IRC Section 41(h)(3) utilize Section D (Lines 33a–36) to elect to apply up to $500,000 of their current-year research credit against employer Social Security and Medicare payroll tax obligations via Form 8974 and Form 941.

Procedural compliance with Form 6765 extends across corporate and pass-through entity structures. Under IRC Section 41(g), 26 CFR § 1.41-7, and the "Who Must File" rules in the Instructions for Form 6765, flow-through entities—specifically partnerships and S corporations—are statutorily required to complete and file Form 6765 at the entity level to establish the validity and quantum of the research credit claim, even when the resulting tax credit flows through via Schedule K and Schedule K-1 to individual partners or shareholders for utilization on their respective income tax returns. Conversely, individual partners, S corporation shareholders, and beneficiaries of estates or trusts whose only source for the Section 41 credit is a pass-through entity are generally not required to complete or attach a separate Form 6765 to their individual returns; instead, they report their distributive share of the credit directly on Form 3800 (General Business Credit), Part III, Line 1c (or Line 4i for eligible small businesses). For estates and trusts, the credit computed on Line 30 of Form 6765 is allocated between the estate or trust and the beneficiaries on Line 31 (reported to beneficiaries on Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), box 13), with the fiduciary's retained share reported on Line 32. Furthermore, under Item B of Form 6765 and IRC Section 41(f)(1), all members of a controlled group of corporations or trades or businesses under common control (regulated under 26 CFR § 1.41-6(a)(3)(ii)) are treated as a single taxpayer for computing the aggregate credit in Section A or Section B, with each member's standalone share determined proportionately to its share of aggregate group QREs and documented via a required group credit attachment.
The Four-Part Test for Qualified Research Activities

Entitlement to report expenditures on Form 6765 depends entirely upon whether the underlying technical activities satisfy the conjunctive Four-Part Test codified in IRC Section 41(d)(1) and detailed in Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a). Failure to substantiate any single statutory pillar invalidates the associated expenditure pool for credit computation purposes on Form 6765.

body.caption: The Four-Part Test for Qualified Research Activities

body.text: Several foundational regulatory standards under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a) govern how the IRS evaluates the Four-Part Test during examinations. First, under the "discovering information" standard of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), a determination that research is undertaken to discover technological information does not require the taxpayer to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering, nor does it require the taxpayer to succeed in developing the new or improved business component. Moreover, under the "patent safe harbor" of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), the issuance of a patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under 35 U.S.C. § 151 (other than a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171) is conclusive evidence that a taxpayer has discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty, though such a patent is not a precondition for credit availability. Second, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a taxpayer may undertake a qualifying process of experimentation even if there is no uncertainty concerning its capability or method of achieving the desired result, so long as the appropriate design of the desired result is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities and the taxpayer conducts an evaluative process capable of assessing alternatives. Third, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the statutory requirement that "substantially all" of the research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, and determined without regard to the 80% employee wage rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under IRC Section 41(d)(3).
Business Component Granularity and the Shrinking-Back Rule

Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(1), the Four-Part Test is not applied to an enterprise's research program in the aggregate; rather, it must be applied separately to each discrete business component. Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B), a business component is statutorily defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Additionally, IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) establishes a special rule for production processes: any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component, and not as part of the business component being produced. Consequently, research activities relating to the development of a manufacturing process are evaluated independently of research activities relating to the development of the product itself, and manufacturing process experimentation may qualify as qualified research even after the underlying product meets functional and economic requirements for commercial sale.

When an overall product or process fails to satisfy the Four-Part Test as a complete system—for example, when a commercial vehicle or enterprise software suite involves predominantly routine assembly alongside isolated technical breakthroughs—the regulatory framework enforces the "shrinking-back" rule codified in Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), if the requirements of IRC Section 41(d) are not met at the level of the discrete overall business component, they are then applied at the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license. This shrinking-back evaluation continues iteratively down through smaller sub-assemblies or elements until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the statutory requirements (including the 80% "substantially all" experimentation threshold) is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails to satisfy the test. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) explicitly specifies that the shrinking-back rule is applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy the requirements of IRC Section 41(d)(1) with respect to the overall business component, and is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility.

The operational convergence between the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) and the rollout of Section E (Line 37) and Section G on the revised Form 6765 fundamentally alters examination defense strategy. Historically, isolating sub-components under the shrinking-back doctrine functioned as a reactive audit defense mechanism deployed only during IRS examination. Under the revised Form 6765, all taxpayers reporting QREs must report the total number of qualifying business components on Section E, Line 37 (beginning in tax year 2024), and non-exempt taxpayers must itemize their business components and allocate QREs by category directly in Section G (required on amended returns claiming new or increased credits, and mandatory on original returns for tax years beginning after 2025 following the IRS's extension of optional transition relief through the 2024 and 2025 tax years). By requiring component-level reporting directly on the tax return, the IRS compels taxpayers to execute shrinking-back isolation prior to filing. If an enterprise aggregates project-wide costs without isolating the specific sub-component where technical uncertainty and systematic experimentation occurred, the filing risks administrative challenge or disallowance.
Classification and Substantiation of Qualified Research Expenditures
Statutory Categories Under IRC Section 41(b)

Form 6765 restricts creditable costs to Qualified Research Expenditures (QREs), defined under IRC Section 41(b)(1) as the sum of in-house research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(1)(A)) and contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(1)(B)) paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. Under IRC Section 41(b)(4), in the case of in-house research expenses, a startup venture is treated as meeting the trade or business requirement of Section 41(b)(1) if, at the time such in-house research expenses are paid or incurred, the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making the expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business of the taxpayer or a controlled group member. In-house research expenses encompass three statutory categories under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)—qualified employee wages, qualified supplies, and off-premises computer rental or lease payments—while third-party expenditures are governed by the contract research rules of IRC Section 41(b)(3) and basic research rules of IRC Section 41(e).

body.text: Wage Attribution and Activity Exclusions

In-house qualified wages typically constitute the largest component of an R&D claim, representing approximately 75% of total QREs in standard software and engineering filings, compared to roughly 15% for supplies and cloud computing and 10% for contract research. Because wage claims dominate credit volume, the classification of employee labor into the three statutory functions under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)—conducting research, directly supervising research, or directly supporting research, which must be reported separately across Columns 50, 51, and 52 of Section G on the revised Form 6765—represents a primary examination focus. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1), "engaging in qualified research" (Column 50) means the actual conduct of qualified research, as in the case of a scientist conducting laboratory experiments. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" (Column 51) means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research, such as an engineering lead or research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments or reviews prototype test parameters, but explicitly excludes supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist. Furthermore, Section E, Line 38 of Form 6765 requires taxpayers to separately disclose the amount of corporate officers' wages included on Line 42. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3), "direct support" (Column 52) covers services in the direct support of persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or persons directly supervising them—such as a machinist machining a part of an experimental model, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research data, or a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results—while excluding general administrative services such as payroll personnel preparing salary checks, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general laboratory cleaning, or corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters. Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), if an employee performs both qualified and nonqualified services, only the wages allocated to qualified services are creditable unless the employee satisfies the "substantially all" wage rule, whereby if at least 80% of the wages paid or incurred for an employee during the taxable year are allocated to qualified services, 100% of that employee's services for the taxable year qualify.

Furthermore, IRC Section 41(d)(4) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c) enumerate specific activities that are categorically excluded from qualifying for the research credit regardless of whether they involve technical personnel. Specifically, taxpayers must exclude any research conducted after commercial production of the business component has begun (IRC § 41(d)(4)(A); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)), which occurs once the component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer, and includes preproduction planning, tooling-up for production, trial production runs, troubleshooting faults in production equipment, accumulating production data, and debugging flaws in a business component. Equally disqualified are activities directed at adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3)), the duplication or reproduction of an existing business component from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4)), and surveys, efficiency studies, management functions or techniques, market research, routine data collection, or routine quality control testing (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)), as well as research conducted in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8)).

With respect to software, geographic boundaries, and third-party funding, the statutory framework enforces strict limitations. Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), the statute excludes research relating to computer software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use in general and administrative functions (such as financial management or human resources) unless the software is developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research, is developed for internal use in a qualifying production process meeting IRC Section 41(d)(1), is part of a new or improved package of hardware and software developed together, or satisfies the regulatory High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii), the HTI test requires demonstrating that the software is innovative (providing a substantial and economically significant reduction in cost or improvement in performance) and involves significant economic risk where substantial technical uncertainty exists at the outset such that resources committed to the project might not be recovered within a reasonable period. For "dual-function software" developed both for internal general and administrative functions and to enable interaction with third parties, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi) and Form 6765 Section G, Column 49(e) allow taxpayers to identify a third-party subset and apply a 25% safe harbor to the remaining dual-function subset if all safe harbor conditions are met. Finally, IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(7) exclude any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any other possession of the United States, and IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9) (cross-referencing 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)) exclude any research funded by another person or governmental entity via grant, contract, or otherwise where the taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the research results or does not bear the financial risk of failure.
Quantitative Mechanics, Calculation Elections, and Reconciled Examples
Regular Credit Method (Section A) Versus Alternative Simplified Credit (Section B)

Taxpayers completing Form 6765 must select between two statutory calculation architectures: the Regular Credit Method in Section A (Lines 1–13) or the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Method in Section B (Lines 14–26). On the revised Form 6765, taxpayers must complete Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary, Lines 42–48)—and Section G, if required—before entering their total QREs from Line 48 onto Line 5 in Section A or Line 20 in Section B.

The Regular Credit Method, codified under IRC Section 41(a)(1) and Section 41(c)(1)–(3), serves as the default statutory framework. Under IRC Section 41(a)(1), the Regular Credit equals 20% of the excess of current-year QREs (Line 5) over the base amount (Line 8), plus 20% of basic research payments to qualified organizations exceeding the qualified organization base period amount (Lines 2–4, IRC § 41(a)(2) and § 41(e)) and 20% of amounts paid or incurred to an energy research consortium (Line 1, IRC § 41(a)(3)). Under IRC Section 41(c)(1) and 41(c)(3)(A), the base amount is calculated by multiplying the taxpayer's Fixed-Base Percentage—defined for existing taxpayers as the historical ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (1984–1988), or determined under the start-up company rules of IRC Section 41(c)(3)(B) (which assign a 3% Fixed-Base Percentage for the first five taxable years with QREs followed by a phased 10-year transition to actual historical QRE-to-gross-receipts ratios), and capped at a maximum of 16% (0.16 on Line 6) under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(C)—by the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the 4 taxable years preceding the credit year (Line 7). Under IRC Section 41(c)(2), in no event may the base amount be less than 50% of current-year QREs (enforced on Lines 10–11 by limiting incremental QREs to the smaller of Line 9 or 50% of Line 5). While the Regular Credit can generate a higher yield for enterprises with low historical base percentages or rapid research expansion relative to gross receipts, the evidentiary burden of substantiating 1984–1988 historical records or multi-year start-up ratios under the consistency rule of IRC Section 41(c)(6) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d) frequently renders Section A impractical for middle-market or newer taxpayers.

To alleviate this historical substantiation barrier, Section B provides the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC). Under IRC Section 41(c)(4)(A), the ASC equals 14% (0.14) of the amount by which current-year QREs (Line 20) exceed 50% of the taxpayer's average QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years.

On Form 6765, Section B executes this calculation by taking total QREs for the prior three tax years on Line 21, dividing Line 21 by 6.0 on Line 22 (equivalent to 50% of the 3-year average), subtracting Line 22 from current-year QREs (Line 20) on Line 23, and multiplying the result by 14% (0.14) on Line 24. Under IRC Section 41(c)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-9(c)(1), if the taxpayer had no QREs in any 1 of those 3 preceding taxable years, the taxpayer skips Lines 22 and 23 and multiplies current-year QREs (Line 20) by 6% (0.06) on Line 24.

The ASC is elected by completing Section B on Form 6765 and attaching the form to a timely filed original return (including extensions) for the tax year to which the election applies. Additionally, under the Form 6765 instructions, an ASC election may be made on an amended return for a tax year only if the taxpayer (and, for a controlled group, every member of the controlled group) had not previously claimed the research credit under any method on an original or amended return for that tax year. Once made, an ASC election applies to the current tax year and all subsequent tax years unless revoked with the consent of the Commissioner. Crucially, under 26 CFR § 1.41-9(b)(3), a taxpayer is deemed to have requested, and to have been granted, the consent of the Commissioner to revoke an ASC election simply by completing the Regular Credit portion (Section A) of Form 6765 on its timely filed original return (including extensions) for that subsequent tax year, although an ASC election may never be revoked on an amended return.

body.text: Interaction of IRC Section 280C and IRC Section 174 / Section 174A Amortization

At the top of Form 6765 in Item A, the taxpayer must indicate ("Yes" or "No") whether it elects the reduced research credit under IRC Section 280C(c)(2). Under IRC Section 280C(c)(2)(C) and the Form 6765 instructions, this election must be made on an original, timely filed tax return (including extensions) and, once made, is irrevocable; it cannot be made retroactively on an amended return.

Under IRC Section 280C(c), a taxpayer is prevented from claiming a double tax benefit (both a full expense deduction or capital account allowance and a full tax credit) for the exact same dollar of research expenditure. If the taxpayer checks "Yes" in Item A to elect the reduced credit under IRC Section 280C(c)(2), the gross research credit determined under IRC Section 41(a) is reduced by the maximum statutory corporate income tax rate under IRC Section 11(b), currently 21%.

On Form 6765, this 21% reduction is computed directly on Line 13 for Section A filers (multiplying Line 12 by 15.8% rather than 20%) and on Line 26 for Section B filers (multiplying Line 25 by 79%). If a taxpayer makes an election in Section D to claim a portion of its research credit as a payroll tax credit, the elected amount is treated as a research credit for purposes of the Section 280C reduced credit rules.

The interaction between the Item A IRC Section 280C election and the capitalization or deductibility of underlying research expenditures reflects both the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) regime and the 2025 legislative enactment of IRC Section 174A under Public Law 119-21 (commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted July 4, 2025). During the 2022 through 2024 tax years under the TCJA amendments to IRC Section 174, specified research and experimental expenditures had to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 5-year period for domestic research and a 15-year period (180 months) for foreign research. For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025, if a taxpayer did not elect the reduced credit under IRC Section 280C(c)(2) and the credit exceeded the amount allowed as a current deduction for qualified research expenses or basic research expenses, the taxpayer was required to reduce the amount chargeable to the capital account for the year for such expenses by that excess amount.

For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, P.L. 119-21 added new IRC Section 174A to the Internal Revenue Code, as detailed in the official What's New and Line 13 instructions for Form 6765. Under IRC Section 174A(a), taxpayers may immediately deduct amounts paid or incurred for domestic research and experimental expenditures in the tax year paid or incurred, or alternatively elect under IRC Section 174A(c) to charge such domestic expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. Meanwhile, foreign research and experimental expenditures remain subject to mandatory capitalization and 15-year amortization under revised IRC Section 174. Concurrently, Section 70302(b)(2)(B) of P.L. 119-21 amended IRC Section 280C(c)(1) so that if a taxpayer checks "No" in Item A (declining the reduced credit election to preserve 100% of the gross tax credit), the taxpayer must reduce its domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A(b) otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to a capital account by the full amount of the research credit allowed under IRC Section 41(a), and attach a statement to its tax return (named Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf if e-filing) listing the reduced deduction or capitalized amounts and identifying the return lines, schedules, or forms where the reductions were made. Additionally, Section 70302(f) of P.L. 119-21 (implemented via IRS Revenue Procedures 2025-28 and 2026-32) provides transition options for taxpayers to recover unamortized domestic research amounts capitalized in tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025.
Reconciled Hypothetical Worked Examples
Hypothetical Example 1: AlgoSoft Corp. QRE Reconciliation and ASC Computation

During the tax year, the enterprise incurs three primary expenditure streams: $850,000 in in-house qualified wages for U.S.-based engineers conducting and directly supervising research, $120,000 for off-premises high-performance computing resources dedicated exclusively to simulation and testing, and $200,000 paid to an unrelated domestic firm for contract research performance evaluations.

Unless the $200,000 figure was already net of the 35% statutory haircut (which would require gross contract payments of $307,692.31, since $200,000 ÷ 0.65 = $307,692.31), including 100% of a $200,000 gross contract invoice overstates eligible QREs by $70,000. Recomputing AlgoSoft Corp.'s eligible QREs by applying the 65% statutory limitation to the $200,000 gross contract research expenditure yields $130,000 in creditable contract research on Line 45 and $1,100,000 in total recomputed QREs on Line 48 (carried to Section B, Line 20).

Assuming for this hypothetical illustration that AlgoSoft Corp. had average annual QREs of $600,000 over the three preceding tax years ($1,800,000 total prior 3-year QREs on Line 21), the Section B Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) and Item A IRC Section 280C reduced credit are computed by establishing a 50% three-year base threshold on Line 22 (Line 21 ÷ 6.0) of $300,000 (0.50 × $600,000), subtracting that base from current-year QREs on Line 23 to determine incremental creditable QREs of $800,000 ($1,100,000 − $300,000, compared to $870,000 unadjusted), multiplying by the 14% statutory ASC rate on Line 24 to arrive at a gross credit of $112,000 (compared to $121,800 unadjusted), and applying the 21% IRC Section 280C reduction (multiplying by 79% on Line 26) to yield a net credit of $88,480 (compared to $96,222 unadjusted).

body.text: Hypothetical Example 2: Credit Impact Simulator

Applying the 65% statutory limitation of IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) to the $50,000 contract research outlay yields $32,500 in creditable contract costs on Line 45 ($50,000 × 0.65). Summing the three components on Line 48 produces a Total QRE pool of $507,500 ($400,000 + $75,000 + $32,500).

Assuming gross revenue equals five times total QREs ($2,537,500) and simplified taxable income equals 20% of gross revenue ($507,500), the baseline 21% corporate income tax liability prior to Form 6765 is $106,575 ($507,500 × 0.21). Applying the $50,750 research credit directly against the tax bill reduces net federal tax liability to $55,825.
The 2024–2026 Form 6765 Structural Overhaul: Sections E, F, and G
Granular Reporting Architecture

The structural overhaul of Form 6765—previewed by the IRS on September 15, 2023 (IR-2023-173), revised after public comment on June 21, 2024 (IR-2024-171), and finalized with extended transition relief in the December 2025 revision of the Instructions for Form 6765 (and IR-2025-99)—introduces top-of-form Items A and B alongside three new reporting sections (Sections E, F, and G) designed to standardize examination-level disclosures on the initial tax return.

cells: Items A & B (Top of Page 1)
Required beginning tax year 2024

Item A: Checkbox ("Yes / No") electing the IRC § 280C reduced credit. Item B: Checkbox ("Yes / No") indicating whether the filer is a member of a controlled group or business under common control under IRC § 41(f)(1), requiring a group credit attachment.
Elevates irrevocable election and controlled group status disclosures to the top of page 1.
Section E (Other Information, Lines 37–41)
Required beginning tax year 2024 if QREs are reported on Line 48

Line 37: Number of business components generating QREs on Line 5 or Line 20. Line 38: Amount of officers' wages included on Line 42. Line 39: Acquisition or disposition of any major portion of a trade or business in the tax year ("Yes / No"). Line 40: Inclusion of any new categories of expenses as current-year QREs ("Yes / No"). Line 41: Election of the ASC 730 Directive ("Yes / No") and entry of Appendix C, Line 19 amount.
Establishes threshold procedural validity, flags officer wage inclusion and base-year consistency adjustments, and identifies large-business safe harbor eligibility upfront.
Section F (QRE Summary, Item A & Lines 42–48)
Required beginning tax year 2024

Item A: Indicates whether the filer is required to complete Section G ("Yes / No"). Disaggregates total QREs across Line 42 (qualified wages), Line 43 (supplies), Line 44 (rental or lease cost of computers), Line 45 (applicable contract research), Line 46 (basic research payments), Line 47 (sum of Lines 45 and 46), and Line 48 (total QREs carried to Line 5 or Line 20).
Eliminates opaque lump-sum QRE reporting and gives IRS classifiers immediate visibility into cost composition prior to credit computation.
Section G (Business Component Info, Columns 49(a)–(f) & 50–56)

Optional for all filers on original returns for tax years beginning before 2026 (covering both 2024 and 2025, extended from the initial 2025 target per IR-2025-99 and Dec. 2025 Instructions); mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (2026) unless exempt. Required for amended returns/AARs claiming new or increased credits.

Requires itemization of the top business components accounting for at least 80% of total QREs in descending order by QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components (the "80%/Top 50" rule), with remaining components reported under "Aggregate Business Components". Captures member EIN (49(a)), PBA code (49(b)), component name/alphanumeric identifier (49(c)), component type (Product, Process, or All Others in 49(d)), software category (IUS, DFS, Non-IUS, or Excepted in 49(e)), information sought to be discovered (49(f), required only on amended returns), direct research wages (Col. 50), direct supervision wages (Col. 51), direct support wages (Col. 52), total wages (Col. 53), supplies (Col. 54), computer rental/lease (Col. 55), and contract research (Col. 56).
Imposes front-loaded audit substantiation; requires contemporaneous project-level time and cost tracking mapping wages by functional role and discrete business component.

body.text: The staged rollout of Section G—initially slated in June 2024 (IR-2024-171) to be optional for tax year 2024 and mandatory for tax year 2025, but subsequently extended by the IRS in October 2025 (IR-2025-99) and the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765 to remain optional for all filers on original returns for tax years beginning before 2026 (both 2024 and 2025) and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (tax year 2026)—creates an essential operational transition window. Moreover, under the official Instructions for Form 6765, even when Section G becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, a taxpayer is exempt from completing Section G if it satisfies either of two exceptions: (1) the taxpayer is a Qualified Small Business (QSB) under IRC Section 41(h)(3) that checks the box in Section D to claim the reduced payroll tax credit; or (2) the taxpayer has total QREs determined at the controlled group level on Line 48 equal to or less than $1,500,000 ($1.5 million) and average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years equal to or less than $50,000,000 ($50 million) (determined under IRC Section 448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph (A)) and is reporting the research credit on an original return. For non-exempt filers, the IRS also narrowed the Section G burden on original returns by making Column 49(f) ("Describe the information sought to be discovered") required only when claiming a refund or credit on an amended return or AAR with a new or increased Section 41 credit, and by capping required component itemization at 80% of total QREs up to a maximum of 50 business components (with any remaining components reported in a single aggregate row labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) and Columns 50–56). Taxpayers utilizing statistical sampling under Revenue Procedure 2011-42 must still report the 80%/Top 50 business components in Section G regardless of which components were selected in the sample, append "sample" to sampled component identifiers in Column 49(c), and attach their sampling plan as Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf. Because employee wages must be disaggregated by both functional role (Columns 50, 51, and 52) and specific business component, legacy compliance workflows that rely on retrospective year-end engineering interviews or high-level cost-center estimates face elevated disallowance risk once Section G becomes mandatory.
Procedural Simplification Under the ASC 730 Directive (Line 41) and Refund Claim Rules

To balance the heightened reporting burden for large enterprises that already maintain rigorous financial accounting controls, Section E, Line 41 of Form 6765 incorporates a procedural pathway for the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) ASC 730 Directive. Specifically, under the Line 41 instructions, a taxpayer is eligible to follow the ASC 730 Directive only if it satisfies three concurrent conditions: (1) it has assets equal to or greater than $10,000,000; (2) it prepares Certified Audited Financial Statements (CAFS) following U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (U.S. GAAP) showing the amount of currently expensed financial statement R&D as a separate line item on the income statement or separately stated in a financial statement note; and (3) it uses these same U.S. GAAP financial statements to reconcile book income to federal tax income on Schedule M-3. Eligible enterprises elect this safe harbor by checking "Yes" on Line 41 of Form 6765, entering the amount from ASC 730 Directive, Appendix C, Line 19 on Line 41 (and optionally attaching Appendices A, B, C, and D), and entering a single "ASC 730 Directive" entry in Section G equal to the Line 41 amount. If that single "ASC 730 Directive" entry in Section G equals at least 80% of the taxpayer's total QREs on Line 48, the taxpayer is not required to report any additional business components in Section G; if it is less than 80%, the taxpayer reports additional business components to satisfy the 80%/Top 50 requirement.

Conversely, taxpayers seeking retroactive research credits via amended returns or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs) that include a Section 41 credit either not reported on the original return or increased from the original return face stringent procedural validation standards. Whereas the prior Form 6765 instructions (i6765--2024.pdf) required five items of information (identifying all business components, all research activities performed, the names or titles/positions of individuals performing each activity, the information each individual sought to discover, and total qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses), the IRS streamlined the refund claim validity rules effective June 18, 2024 (IR-2024-171 and current i6765.pdf) to require three items of information with the amended return or AAR: (1) identifying the business components to which the research credit claim relates, (2) for each business component, identifying all research activities performed and describing the information sought to be discovered by completing Section G, Column 49(f), and (3) providing total qualified employee wage, supply, computer rental, and contract research expenses via Form 6765. When e-filing an amended return or AAR, the taxpayer must name the required substantiation attachment Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf, and if submitting a credit study or other documents, must identify the exact pages containing the required information in an attachment named Form6765Study.pdf. Furthermore, partnerships subject to the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 (BBA partnerships) cannot file amended returns and must instead file an AAR accompanied by Forms 8985 and 8986, while partners of a BBA partnership attach Form 8978 to their returns.
Small Business Monetization: Section D Payroll Tax Credit Election
Statutory Criteria and Discrepancy Analysis

For pre-revenue or early-stage enterprises that incur substantial domestic R&D expenses but lack current federal income tax liability, a General Business Credit carryforward on Form 3800 provides no immediate cash liquidity. Section D of Form 6765 (Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Election and Payroll Tax Credit, Lines 33a–36) addresses this constraint by enabling a Qualified Small Business (QSB) to elect under IRC Section 41(h) and IRC Section 3111(f) to apply a portion of its research credit against its federal employer payroll tax liability.

A corporation (including an S corporation), partnership, or other person (excluding tax-exempt organizations under IRC Section 501) is a QSB only if it satisfies two exact statutory requirements: (1) it has gross receipts of less than $5,000,000 ($5 million) for the current tax year; and (2) it had no gross receipts for any tax year preceding the 5-tax-year period ending with the current tax year. Thus, the statutory ceiling under IRC Section 41(h)(3)(A)(i) is strictly less than $5,000,000 (not "up to $5,000,000"), and the official Form 6765 instructions clarify why IRC Section 448(c) is cross-referenced in the statute: "gross receipts" for the QSB test are determined using the definition of gross receipts in IRC Section 448(c)(3) (without regard to subparagraph (A) thereof) and Treasury Regulations 26 CFR § 1.448-1T(f)(2)(iii) and (iv) (taking into account aggregate gross receipts across all trades or businesses under common control and annualizing gross receipts for short tax years of less than 12 months), rather than importing the inflation-adjusted $25,000,000 to $30,000,000 general small business gross receipts threshold of IRC Section 448(c) or the Section 41(c)(6) definition of gross receipts.

Under the Instructions for Form 6765, the Section D election must be made on or before the due date of the originally filed income tax return (including extensions), cannot be made for a tax year if an election was already made for 5 or more preceding tax years, is made at the entity level for partnerships and S corporations, and may be revoked only with IRS consent. On Section D of Form 6765, an electing QSB checks the box on Line 33a (and Line 33b if payroll tax is reported on a different EIN), enters the portion of Line 28 elected as a payroll tax credit (not to exceed $500,000) on Line 34, enters the General Business Credit carryforward from the current year on Line 35 (skipped by partnerships and S corporations, while C corporations and individuals must complete Form 3800 before completing Section D), and enters the final allowable payroll tax credit on Line 36—equal to the smaller of Line 28 or Line 34 for partnerships and S corporations, or the smallest of Line 28, Line 34, or Line 35 for all other filers.
Quarterly Utilization Mechanics Under the Inflation Reduction Act

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) expanded the liquidity benefit of Section D by doubling the maximum annual payroll tax credit election from $250,000 to $500,000 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022. Once elected on Section D of Form 6765 (Line 36) and filed with the annual income tax return, the payroll tax credit is monetized on a quarterly basis by completing Form 8974 (Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities) and attaching it to the employer's employment tax return—most commonly Form 941 (Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return), or annual Form 943 or Form 944—beginning in the first calendar quarter that starts after the date on which the taxpayer files its federal income tax return reflecting the election. If the QSB uses a third-party payer or Non-Certified Professional Employer Organization (PEO) that files an aggregate Form 941, a separate Form 8974 must be completed and attached for each client taking the credit alongside Schedule R (Form 941).

For calendar quarters beginning in 2023 and thereafter, IRC Section 3111(f)(1)–(4) and Part 2 of Form 8974 apply the credit in a sequential two-tier offset structure. In the first tier (IRC § 3111(f)(1)(A); Form 8974, Lines 8–12), the credit reduces the employer's share of Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (Social Security) tax (calculated on Form 8974, Line 11 as 50% of total Social Security tax on wages and tips from Form 941, Lines 5a and 5b) up to a maximum of $250,000 per quarter (per IRC § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(I)). In the second tier (IRC § 3111(f)(1)(B); Form 8974, Lines 13–17), any remaining credit for the quarter after reducing the employer's share of Social Security tax up to the $250,000 limit is applied directly against the employer's share of Hospital Insurance (Medicare) tax for that quarter (calculated on Form 8974, Line 15 as 50% of total Medicare tax from Form 941, Line 5c). Finally, under IRC Section 3111(f)(3) and the Form 8974 instructions, any credit amount exceeding both employer Social Security and Medicare payroll tax liabilities for the quarter is carried forward automatically on Form 8974, Part 1, Column (g) to offset employer payroll tax liabilities in the succeeding calendar quarter, and under IRC Section 3111(f)(4), the payroll tax credits allowed do not reduce the employer's federal income tax deduction under Chapter 1 for employer Social Security and Medicare taxes.
Strategic Compliance Recommendations

To mitigate examination exposure and preserve full credit monetization under the revised Form 6765 architecture, enterprises should execute a four-part operational compliance strategy derived directly from the statutory and regulatory framework:

items: Deploy Component-Level Cost Accounting Ahead of the 2026 Section G Mandate: Tax and engineering departments should utilize the extended 2024–2025 optional transition period (under IR-2025-99 and the December 2025 Form 6765 instructions) to align internal accounting and project-tracking codes directly with discrete "business components" as defined under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B). Proactively mapping sub-components under the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) ensures that if an overarching commercial release includes routine adaptation or post-production maintenance, qualifying experimental sub-assemblies remain cleanly segregated to satisfy the 80% "substantially all" experimentation threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) and the "80%/Top 50" reporting rules of Section G.

Reconfigure Payroll and Time-Tracking Taxonomies for Three-Tier Wage Disaggregation: Because employee wage QREs in Section G must be substantiated by both discrete business component and statutory service tier across Column 50 (actual conduct), Column 51 (direct first-line supervision), and Column 52 (direct support) under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c), organizations should implement contemporaneous digital time-allocation protocols that distinguish between these three functions. Capturing technical narratives alongside time logs eliminates the audit vulnerability associated with retrospective percentage estimates, identifies employees meeting the 80% "substantially all" wage threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), and defends first-line technical supervision claims against reclassification as upper-level management or corporate officer wages disclosed on Section E, Line 38.

Institutionalize Joint Technical-Tax Substantiation Protocols: Organizations should establish a formal corporate R&D documentation policy pairing engineering and scientific leads continuously with tax personnel so that contemporaneous evidence of technical uncertainty and systematic experimentation—such as hypothesis logs, simulation failures, prototype test results, and architecture trade-off analyses—is archived concurrently with development sprints. This contemporaneous archive is essential for classifying software under Section G, Column 49(e) (IUS, DFS, Non-IUS, and Excepted), segregating off-premises research computer leases under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4) on Line 44, verifying third-party contract research agreements under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) on Line 45, and satisfying the Column 49(f) narrative and Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf requirements governing amended returns and AARs.

Execute Multi-Year Financial Modeling Across Calculation, Section 280C, Section 174A, and Line 41 Elections: Prior to finalizing Form 6765 each year, tax departments should execute multi-year financial modeling to compare the yield, volatility, and compliance burden of the Regular Credit (Section A) against the Alternative Simplified Credit (Section B), accounting for the deemed-consent revocation procedures of 26 CFR § 1.41-9(b)(3). Simultaneously, financial modeling must evaluate the net cash-flow interaction between the irrevocable Item A IRC Section 280C(c)(2) 21% reduced credit election and domestic research deductibility or optional 60-month amortization under new IRC Section 174A (enacted by P.L. 119-21 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, alongside 15-year foreign research amortization under IRC Section 174 and 2022–2024 transition recovery options under Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32), as well as eligibility for the LB&I ASC 730 Directive safe harbor on Line 41 for taxpayers with $10,000,000 or more in total assets.
